courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
md: Patches end a bug; detections outlive it. Word starting msdt.exe was abnormal before May 2022 and is still abnormal now, so the behaviour rule keeps catching the next abuse of a protocol handler.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Never use one keystream twice. Reusing keystream material across files turns any file whose original you hold into a key for others. Sound designs encrypt each file with its own key from a proper cipher and protect the master secret with public-key encryption.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
md: A full compromise of a hardened platform is a chain, usually renderer RCE plus sandbox escape plus kernel bug. Each extra wall forces another 0-day, and each stage is a separate chance to detect or break the attack.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Stickers, turtles and malware: attacks outside the lab
md: Physical and problem-space attacks are real but constrained: they must survive transformations and keep the object working. Real attackers mostly use cheap manual tricks found by probing. Design so that one fooled model is not one fooled system.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Training with differential privacy: DP-SGD and its price
md: An epsilon without its delta, its unit (one record, one user?) and its accountant is not a privacy claim. Ask what one 'record' means: if a user contributes 500 records, record-level DP says little about that user.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Detecting C2: beacons, egress and fingerprints
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, monitoring agents and chat clients poll on timers too. A beacon score is a hunting lead, ranked with rarity of the destination and the type of host, not an alert on its own. Allowlist known pollers by destination and process, and review the list, because an intruder can hide behind an allowlisted name.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Distortion-free per token is not the same as diverse. Because r is a deterministic function of the key and the last few tokens, the same prompt and context always produce the same output, which a user who asks twice can notice. The next block shows Kuditipudi et al.'s fix.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Replay is open-loop: the program's computation between calls is gone, so cache contents and timing differ, and cycles per call in replay are not the application's allocator time. Use replay for memory comparisons and relative call costs, and confirm with a real run.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: Anomalies in the history contaminate the baseline. If last Tuesday's outage is in the training window, a mean-based baseline and standard deviation absorb it and become blind to the next one. That is why both the toy baseline here and S-H-ESD use medians and MAD: one bad day out of 27 does not move a same-hour median.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Rate limits, quotas and resource exhaustion
md: Limits enforced only at one gateway disappear on any path that skips the gateway: a beta host, an internal route, an old API version. Apply the limit in the service, or make sure every route goes through the gateway.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
md: A JWT is readable by anyone and trustworthy only after the signature and claims are checked by the receiver, using keys and rules the receiver chose. Everything in it, including the header, is attacker-controlled until then.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: A programme is owners plus deadlines plus measurement. For every activity in this course, ask three questions: which named person or team does it, by when, and which number shows that it actually happens?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SAST in CI: false positives, triage and developer trust
md: A suppression is a risk acceptance. If anyone can add `nosemgrep` without review, the cheapest way to pass CI is to silence the tool. Route suppressions in sensitive paths through CODEOWNERS (lesson 1) so AppSec sees them.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Patch SLAs, exceptions and the race after disclosure
md: An exception without an expiry date is a permanent vulnerability with paperwork. Track exceptions as their own metric: how many, how old, and how many were renewed more than once.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: Tuning tradeoffs follow directly from the passes. Rare checkpoints and slow background page writes make the smallest recLSN old, so redo scans more log. Long-running transactions make undo long and keep old log needed. Frequent checkpoints shorten redo but cost extra log and page writes at runtime.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: A semaphore limits **how many** requests are in flight, not **how fast** they start. Concurrency times the inverse of latency gives your request rate, so when latency drops (short prompts, cache hits) the same semaphore sends requests faster. Pair it with a rate limiter, covered next.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs
md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
md: A salt does nothing against an attacker focused on *one* account. With a single salted SHA-256 hash, the attacker simply runs their guess list with that salt at full GPU speed. Salting is necessary but not sufficient: the hash must also be slow, which is lesson 5.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
md: Training people to spot fake pages helps, but NIST defines phishing resistance as working *without relying on the user's vigilance*. The Twitter employees were busy, remote, and called by someone who knew personal details about them.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
md: An LLM judge grading an LLM agent can share its blind spots. Validate the judge against human labels (as JudgeEval does), keep humans testing edge cases, and read transcripts: a high score with a shortcut in the logs is a failed run.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: C++ binaries: name mangling, vtables and RTTI
md: RTTI is useful evidence, not proof. Typeinfo name strings like `N3geo4RectE` survive stripping, and the vtables they point to let you list every polymorphic class and its virtual methods. But builds can disable RTTI (`-fno-rtti`), and malware authors can pick misleading class names. Confirm with constructors (which store the vptr) and with the code itself.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (queries Q times keys K, then the attention weights times values V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 7 covers.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog, whose optimization manuals measure these costs on real chips, gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Chromium's processes: browser, renderer, GPU, network, utility
md: A sandboxed renderer should never be the parent of a shell or any other ordinary program. A process tree where a renderer (or the GPU or network process) starts something new is one of the clearest endpoint signals that a sandbox has failed.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Case: CVE-2023-4863, one image library inside everything
md: A bug in a shared parsing library is a supply-chain event. Inventory where the library is linked (browsers, Electron apps, image tools, mobile apps), not just which browser version users run. CISA's catalog entry for this CVE says it "can affect applications that use the WebP Codec".

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Bloom filters only help point lookups. A range scan must open every run that overlaps the range and merge them, so the RocksDB guide counts scan read amplification as (L0 files) + (non-empty levels). Tiered layouts with many runs pay most for scans.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
md: Real systems combine a cheap recency approximation with a second signal: PostgreSQL uses counts plus per-operation rings, InnoDB uses a two-segment list with a time threshold, and 2Q and LRU-2 use a remembered first reference. The common goal: a page must prove reuse before it can displace the hot set.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: High availability is not disaster recovery: GitLab, January 2017
md: High availability copies every change, good or bad, as fast as it can; it protects against component failure. Disaster recovery needs copies that did *not* follow the bad change: point-in-time backups or snapshots, kept separately. Ask of every copy: which failures does it survive?

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When the building burns: OVHcloud 2021 and DR site strategies
md: A disaster recovery copy must sit outside the failure domain of the disaster: another building is not enough if the site is isolated, another zone is not enough if the control plane deletes both. Pick a site or cloud strategy by RTO and cost, and fail over with the most available mechanisms.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention (methods and kernels such as FlashAttention that make attention cheaper or faster) helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: A common misconception is that memory cost is proportional to the bytes your code reads. It is proportional to the **lines it touches**. Reading 8 bytes from each of 1,000 scattered lines moves 64,000 bytes through the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
md: Collapsing chains is not free. If the real model really runs a mutually reinforcing loop (the paper sees Copenhagen and Denmark features exciting each other with per-layer transcoders), a CLT can hide it. Simpler graphs can mean less faithful graphs.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Lab: trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer
md: Graph, then labels, then interventions, then a report that names its own gaps. The graph proposes; only the measured change in the real model, including the swaps that fail, counts as evidence.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code
md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
md: Prevention lives in code (encode, sanitise, safe sinks, tokens, allowlists). Detection lives mostly in the browser (CSP and Trusted Types reports) and in monitoring of what your pages load. A team that only watches server logs is blind to DOM XSS and skimmers.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Reading CloudTrail like a responder: who really made this call?
md: Misconception: "the event names the role, so the role's owner did it". A role is a costume many identities can put on. Attribution needs the chain: issued key to used key, back to a long-term credential, a federated sign-in or a workload.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles
md: Misconception: "the CloudTrail logs show no data access, so the cloud was not affected". If an attacker held a vault administrator account, every stored credential must be treated as exposed. Absence of use in the logs you have narrows the impact; it does not remove the need to rotate.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Graphing attack paths: role chains, PMapper and Access Analyzer
md: Least privilege is a property of the graph, not of one policy. Ask "who can reach this role or this data, through any chain?", fix the cheapest edge on each path, and rerun the analysis after every IAM change.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
md: Scanners produce a lot of findings, and most teams drown in them. Rank by what an attacker could do: public exposure of sensitive data, wildcard IAM on roles reachable from the internet, IMDSv1 on internet-facing instances and disabled logging come before "detailed monitoring is off". A posture tool is only as good as the triage behind it.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Five criteria on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3, BIC with a variance floor says k = 3, and the gap statistic says one cluster. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
md: Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Assume the model will sometimes be wrong or hijacked, and design so that it does not matter much: isolate the machine, keep secrets and broad network access out of it, require a human for irreversible actions, and check every action before it runs.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: Use loom to search **schedules** of a tiny test exhaustively, and TSan to check **ordering** on real runs of the whole program. Neither proves correctness alone; together they cover far more than any number of stress runs.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
md: W + R greater than N guarantees that a read sees every *completed* write. Linearizability also needs reads to agree with each other while a write is in flight. ABD gets that by making each read finish only after its result sits on a quorum.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
md: A `should` clause is not an OR filter when the query also has a `filter` or `must` clause, because minimum_should_match then defaults to 0. Putting a hard requirement in `should` silently turns it into a mere preference. Set `minimum_should_match` explicitly if you need at least one of several options to match.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: Common mistakes. **CP-SAT works over integers only**: a coefficient like 0.5 must be scaled (multiply the constraint by 2). A status of `FEASIBLE` after a time limit is not a proof of optimality, and `UNKNOWN` is not a proof of infeasibility. With more than one worker, runs are not guaranteed to be repeatable; tests and demos often set `num_workers = 1`.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
md: privileged, extra capabilities, hostPath, runtime sockets, hostPID and hostNetwork each turn a container back into a process on the host. If a workload asks for one, ask why, and isolate it if the answer is real.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Misconception: "we enforce Restricted, so pods are safe". PSA checks pod fields only. It does not check the image, RBAC, network policy or which Secrets are mounted, and namespaces or users can be exempted in its configuration. It is one layer.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Misconception: "we have audit logging, so we would see an attack". The audit log sees API requests. An attacker who never calls the API server (kubelet exec, a runtime escape, a miner in an existing pod) leaves no audit events. Pair it with node-level runtime detection and network flow logs.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Model the state as a fixed schema where every slot is present and null means unconstrained. Each turn applies one of a few explicit operations per slot, and carryover is the default.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Misconception: "if every step of the CoT is correct, the CoT explains the answer." Turpin et al. found unfaithful CoTs with no obvious errors. Checking that reasoning is *valid* tests plausibility. Only a counterfactual (change an input the CoT ignores and see if the answer moves) tests faithfulness.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Two kernels at once: concurrency, stream priorities, comm overlap
md: A second stream gives a kernel *permission* to run beside another; free SM resources decide whether it *does*. Priority decides who gets the next free SM, never who gets evicted. Communication overlaps compute only when there is independent compute to overlap it with, which usually means splitting the batch.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
md: A block cipher on its own encrypts exactly one block. Real messages are many blocks, and how you chain them (the **mode**) decides whether patterns leak. Calling raw AES block by block is the mistake of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
md: Strong algorithms fail through their callers. When reviewing crypto, ask what the attacker can choose, what they can observe, what must never repeat, what is compared, and whether each key has one job. The rest of this course is those five questions applied to real failures.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
md: A random-looking key tells you nothing about how many keys were possible. Weak keys from Debian, Android and the Ps and Qs devices all looked perfectly random one at a time; the problem only shows when you compare many.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: Pooling does not make stranding vanish. In the toy pooled design, host D still has 64 GB of local DRAM it cannot sell. Pooling helps because the *peaks* of different hosts rarely line up, so a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of per-host slack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
md: Two failure modes for beginners: thinking "no damage, no crime" ((a)(2) only needs access plus obtaining information), and thinking "no money taken, no loss" (response costs are loss).

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Budapest Convention (2001): common offences (Articles 2 to 6, with a carve-out for authorised testing), procedural powers, and cooperation: fast preservation (up to 90 days domestically; at least 60 days for a foreign request) and a 24/7 contact network.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Before monitoring: who authorised it, were users informed, and is this the least intrusive data that answers the question? Prefer metadata to content, pseudonymise identifiers, limit retention, and never repurpose what you saw.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Authority, jurisdiction, minimum data, other laws, harm to people, records and reporting. Run all six before you touch what is not yours, and keep the evidence that you did.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: Modern mixtures are schedules. A long first stage uses a broad mix; a short final stage, run while the learning rate decays to zero, upweights the best small sources (repeated a few times if needed). The same short anneal doubles as a cheap test of whether a new dataset is worth adding.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
md: Measure what the hot path *reads repeatedly*. Splitting the search key from its payload shrinks the working set the loop revisits, which often matters more than the miss count of a single call.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field
md: "Encrypted at rest" in a compliance checklist usually means disk, storage or TDE encryption. It answers stolen hardware and copied backups. It does nothing against SQL access, application bugs or stolen credentials, which is how most data is actually taken.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Media sanitisation: clear, purge and destroy (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)
md: On SSDs and flash, never trust file shredders or multi-pass overwrites. Use the drive's sanitise command or cryptographic erase (and verify the result), or physically destroy it. In the cloud, crypto erase of keys you control is usually the only purge you can perform.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: DNS canaries: tripwires that escape locked-down networks
md: A DNS canary trades detail for reach: it fires from almost anywhere, but tells you only that the token was resolved and which resolver asked. Pair it with internal resolver logs to find the host.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Building batch-invariant kernels: RMSNorm, matmul and attention
md: A kernel is batch-invariant when every output element is reduced in an order fixed by that element alone. RMSNorm: one row per core, idle cores accepted. Matmul: one tile configuration, no split-K or stream-K. Attention: one KV layout written before the kernel, and a fixed split size, never a fixed split count.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: A passing simulation is only as good as its fault model and its oracles. If your simulated disk never loses unsynced writes, you have not tested crash recovery; if no oracle checks liveness, a stuck cluster passes.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
md: Do not "fix" drift by blindly running apply from the drift job. The job holds a read-only role on purpose, and an automatic revert can undo an emergency change in the middle of an incident. Alert, decide, then go through the normal pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency): lesson 1's estimate gives an H100 room for about 295 tokens per pass at the cost of one. Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
md: At scale, disaggregation is about shapes: prefill and decode want different expert-parallel widths, communication modes and batch sizes, and their best ratio moves with the traffic mix. Size pools from each phase's share of GPU time, resize on predicted rather than current load, and expect decode itself to split further into attention and FFN.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
md: Turning a seized phone off "to preserve it" can move it from AFU to BFU and lock most of its data away for good. Decide on power, isolation and extraction before you touch it, and document every interaction.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
md: Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every **offline** method (one that trains on a fixed dataset instead of sampling new answers from the policy), DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: PQXDH: a post-quantum first message, and what formal analysis found
md: PQXDH makes recorded first messages safe against a future quantum computer by adding a KEM secret to the X3DH KDF. Hybrids help only if each key is unambiguously typed and every component is bound into the derived key.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Group chats: pairwise fan-out, sender keys, and who decides membership
md: Showing "Mallory joined" in the timeline is not a fix. In large groups nobody reads membership events, as the Matrix researchers point out in lesson 18. Membership must be cryptographically authorised, or at least require explicit acceptance before keys are sent.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Lawful access and client-side scanning
md: Mathematically there is no way to let a third party inspect E2EE content "only for bad content": either something outside the two ends learns about plaintext, or it does not. Every proposal moves that knowledge somewhere (a key escrow, a scanner, a backup), and that place becomes the new target.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
md: MFA protects the login, not the session. Anything that leaks or steals a session token after login bypasses MFA completely, which is why session lifetime, session binding and killing sessions after an incident matter.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
md: A device that can no longer be patched, or that you cannot trust after a compromise, is not a vulnerability to manage: it is a replacement to schedule. Track support dates like expiry dates and replace before them.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
md: Check the value you will use, in the form you will use it, after every step that can change its meaning. Anything else is checking a different string.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577
md: Escaping does not save you here. WorstFit shows arguments that were correctly quoted and escaped in UTF-16 becoming mis-split after conversion, because a fullwidth quote or a yen sign turns into a real quote or backslash after the escaping already ran.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
md: EDR does not replace logs or antivirus. It adds a recorder on every endpoint, a fleet-wide brain, and a remote hand. Each of the three can fail separately: no sensor, no data; no analytics, no alert; no one watching, no response.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Attack surface reduction rules: blocking risky behaviours
md: Exclusions are the quiet failure. Microsoft warns that excluding files or folders "can severely reduce ASR rule protection" and that excluded files run with **no reports or events recorded**. An exclusion for a whole folder such as a user-writable tools directory turns a rule off for anything an attacker can drop there.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
md: Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: An app is defined once (application object, home tenant) and instantiated per tenant (service principal). Credentials live with the definition, permissions with the instance. Anyone who can add a credential to a powerful app becomes that app.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: In device code flow, the tokens go to whoever started the flow, not to whoever signed in. Block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy except where a known device needs it, and hunt for deviceCode in sign-in logs followed by device registrations.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Every component that bridges AD to Entra ID (the sync server and its accounts, PTA agents, the AZUREADSSOACC key, AD FS) can create or impersonate cloud identities. Treat each as Tier 0, roll the Seamless SSO key at least every 30 days, and keep cloud admins cloud-only.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
md: Common misconception: "ASLR makes the overflow fail." It does not stop the corruption at all; the attacker still overwrites the pointer. ASLR only makes the *value* they write likely to be wrong. Anything that tells them the right value (next lesson) cancels it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
md: Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers (queues that hold a core's writes while it keeps running) and out-of-order execution (running later independent instructions while an earlier one waits), prefetch lines before they are asked for, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
md: A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Below the operating system: why boot code is the deepest foothold
md: A check can only be as trustworthy as the code that performs it. Boot security is a chain: each stage verifies or measures the next, and the chain is only as strong as its first link and its weakest check.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Remote attestation: quotes, nonces and what a verifier can trust
md: Freshness is part of the claim. A valid signature over good PCRs only proves the machine was good *at some point*. The nonce binds the quote to this request.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 math tricks: software exp2, conditional rescaling
md: Misconception: "the final division by $l$ fixes any scaling." It cancels a factor shared by $O$ and $l$, but not a weight that was clipped when $P$ was cast to a 16-bit or 8-bit type before $PV$. That is why $\tau$ is bounded by the type's range.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: MLA in FlashInfer: attention over a compressed latent cache
md: Absorbed MLA is multi-query attention over a 576-wide shared row: 1,152 bytes per token per layer and 128 query rows per byte. FlashInfer serves it with the same page table, plan/run and merge machinery, through BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper with separate ckv and kpe pages.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLC: breadth-first search over every reachable state
md: Liveness is only checked if you ask. In the CACM paper's table of results, a lock-free data structure spec "improved confidence" but missed a liveness bug because liveness was not checked. Also remember the bounded model: no error at N = 3 says nothing about N = 4.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
md: Verification moves trust from "we tested enough" to "the spec says the right thing". Spend your review effort on the spec: the invariants, the environment actions you modeled, and every assumption or trusted function.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
md: A 2x faster GEMM is not a 2x faster step: the speedup is capped by the non-GEMM share of time and eaten into by casting overhead. FP8 GEMM inputs also save almost no memory; the bytes live in master weights, gradients and optimizer state, and in communication, which need their own FP8 treatment (shared scales, automatic scaling).

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: "The data was public anyway" was not a defence. Each field may be visible on a profile, but linking a phone number to a name at scale creates a new data set the users never published. Regulators judge the feature design, not just whether a password was stolen.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: Each verification step also costs honest people: those without a phone of their own, without a bank card, or without the right documents. Put the expensive steps in front of the high-value actions they protect, and offer an alternative path.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Do not train on chargebacks as if they arrived on the day of the payment. Recent payments look clean simply because their disputes have not arrived yet; a model trained on last week's data learns that last week had no fraud.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Enforcement, explanations and appeals
md: Enforce on a proportionate ladder, give a statement of the policy and behaviour (not the detector's thresholds), let a different person review appeals, and treat overturns as labels.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
md: After fsync fails on buffered data, assume the dirty data is gone. Do not retry and continue: recover from a log you know is durable. That is why PostgreSQL's [data_sync_retry](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-error-handling.html) defaults to off, which turns such a failure into a PANIC and a WAL replay.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: To compare two fuzzing setups: 30 or more runs each, at least 24 hours, the same documented seeds, a statistical test, and bugs counted by distinct fixes. Anything less is an anecdote.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Publishing a working exploit is a separate, debated decision (OWASP notes both sides). It is never needed to get a memory-safety bug fixed: the sanitizer report and minimised input are proof. This course's path ends at the fix and the advisory.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
md: Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Misconception: latitude and longitude are x and y on a flat grid. They are angles on a sphere. Any shortcut that treats them as planar (Euclidean distance on degrees, fixed-size degree boxes) is wrong by a factor of $1/\cos\varphi$ in the east-west direction and breaks at 180 degrees longitude and near the poles.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Reusing a freed block on the same stream is safe without synchronization because stream order already serializes the old and new users. Cross-stream reuse needs events: record_stream in PyTorch, event dependencies in cudaMallocAsync pools.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: **Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
md: Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: The headline result is GraphRAG versus vector RAG on global sensemaking questions: 72 to 83% comprehensiveness win rates on Podcast. Against map-reduce over raw text, the advantage is small; the bigger win there is token cost at query time.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns
md: Hindsight makes every incident look obvious. At the time, the engineers involved were usually competent people working with the knowledge and trade-offs of their day. Read each case asking "what would have had to be true for this to be caught?", not "how could they be so careless?"

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book
md: Mass mailers exploited trust in three things at once: the sender (a friend's address), the file (a hidden extension) and the program (Outlook let scripts read addresses and send mail). Each fix removed one trust: show real extensions, block executable attachments, and make programs ask before using your address book or sending.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update
md: "It looked like ransomware, so paying would have restored our data" was wrong here. Kaspersky showed the attackers could not decrypt the disks. Classify destructive incidents by what the code does, not by what the ransom screen says.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
md: A percentage in parentheses after a `perf stat` line, like `(74.98%)`, means that event ran only that fraction of the time and was scaled. Treat such numbers as estimates, and be most suspicious when the workload has phases.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
md: An enclave or TEE protects against software that cannot reach its memory. It does not remove side channels: if enclave code runs on the same core as the attacker, its cache footprint, branch history and timing are as observable as any other program's. Enclave code must still be constant-time.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: HTTP/2 framing, and how downgrading brings desync back
md: HTTP/2 removes framing ambiguity only while the request stays HTTP/2. Every downgrade to HTTP/1.1 must enforce RFC 9113's rules before writing text: content-length equals the DATA total, no connection-specific fields, no CR, LF or NUL in names or values.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
md: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on different documents. BM25 misses paraphrases; dense retrieval blurs exact identifiers, codes and rare names. Fusing the lists recovers documents either one would miss and promotes documents both agree on.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Federation replaces many passwords with one trust decision per app: accept whatever this IdP's key signs, after checking it was meant for me, now. Every attack in this course breaks one of those three parts: the key, the checks, or the moment.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
md: Treat the IdP's signing keys and the configuration that says which IdPs and keys are trusted as tier 0 (Microsoft's name for the assets that control every identity in an organisation): the same protection as domain controllers (the servers that hold Active Directory's accounts and keys). Anyone who can change either can become any user without touching a password.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule
md: Session security cannot exceed device security. PAM, bastions and JIT protect the path; the PAW protects its start. Decide at a policy engine using identity, device and approval together, issue short-lived credentials, and enforce at one point.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
md: Isolating a host is not the same as stopping damage on it. NIST's example: a process that pings a remote host and, when the ping fails after disconnection, encrypts the disk. Capture what you need first when you can.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels
md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS (few I/O operations per second), bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device secrets: per-device keys, secure elements and House of Keys
md: Design rule: the worst outcome of fully compromising one unit should be the loss of that unit. Achieve it with per-device keys generated on the device, public keys in the cloud, and no shared secrets in firmware.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
md: `--disable-proto` is a useful second layer, not the fix: our test shows the `constructor.prototype` route still pollutes with it on. Fix the write (own keys, refused names, null-prototype objects); add the flag as defence in depth.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: The server-client boundary: Server Actions, secrets and bundles
md: Do not treat arguments of a Server Action as typed or trusted because TypeScript declared their types. TypeScript types disappear at run time; the POST body can contain anything. Validate arguments with a schema inside the action, exactly as you would for a REST endpoint.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
md: Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: When the signing pipeline is the target: ADV220005
md: Every signature-based trust decision has an upstream: the people and processes that issue signatures. When that upstream is abused (stolen keys, fraudulent developer accounts), revocation, deny lists and inventory-based allowlists are what still work.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
md: These numbers are one run: one small model, one synthetic task, a 2K-token prompt and 50 trials per bar, so other keys or filler can move a bar by several points. They show failure modes, not rankings: repeated filler is unusually easy for StreamingLLM and unusually hard for windowed voting. Rerun the harness on your own prompts, lengths and model before choosing a method.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Build Coconut: stage data, loss mask and the multi-pass forward
md: A Coconut training step is n + 1 cached forward passes whose logits are joined into one loss. Gradients flow back through every pass, so time and stored activations both grow with the number of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
md: The WY form and the UT transform turn C sequential rank-1 updates into one small C x C triangular solve plus matmuls ($KK^\top$, $TK$, $TV$, $WS^\top$, $QK^\top$, $D^\top K$). Only that solve and the hand-off of the state between chunks remain sequential.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Setuid, setgid and sticky: borrowed privilege and its bugs
md: "It is only a local bug" is a dangerous phrase. Local privilege escalation means any foothold, such as a hijacked web application running as `www-data`, becomes root. PwnKit and Dirty COW both needed only an ordinary account.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: Learn the shape of four lines: Failed password, Accepted (password or publickey), sudo COMMAND, and sudo denials. Then look for sequences, not single lines: failures then success from one source, and a fresh login followed by privileged changes.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: Every directive can break something: `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` breaks JIT runtimes, `ProtectProc=invisible` can break tools that inspect other processes, `ProcSubset=pid` is, per the manual, not suitable for most non-trivial programs. Add directives one at a time on a test host and watch the journal for denials.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco watches system calls. In April 2025 the security company ARMO showed a proof-of-concept rootkit that does its file and network work through io_uring (lesson 6), and reported Falco's default rules did not see it. Lesson 13 covers what that means for every syscall-based sensor.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: "Installed" is the most common false comfort in patch reports. The xz-utils and regreSSHion fixes did nothing for a daemon that kept running the old code; libraries need service restarts and kernels need reboots or livepatches. Report on what is running.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
md: Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
md: Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks
md: A serving benchmark is a curve, not a number: sweep the request rate with random arrivals, and at each rate report p50 and p99 of TTFT, TPOT and ITL plus goodput under your SLOs. Throughput equals offered load until saturation, so the interesting part is where latency bends.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Who goes next: priority, fairness and length-aware scheduling
md: Admission decides whether a request fits; ordering decides who waits. FCFS is simple but lets long jobs block short ones. SJF by predicted rank cuts mean latency, VTC shares service fairly between clients, and explicit priorities protect interactive traffic, each with a guard against starvation.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals, test sets of inputs with known good answers). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates. Dropping them also silently biases every count you compute afterwards.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
md: Never write secrets into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists data to exclude or mask: passwords, access tokens, session identifiers (hash them if you need to follow a session), encryption keys, connection strings and sensitive personal data. Logs are copied widely, so anything in them leaks widely.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
md: Every allowlist entry is a promise that this pattern will never be malicious. Prefer fields the attacker cannot set (exact path in a protected folder, code-signing publisher, asset group from your inventory) over fields they can (process name, command-line text, user agent, file name).

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
md: Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
